bib.title: MemCollab: Cross-Model Memory Collaboration via Contrastive Trajectory Distillation

legacy_report:
SOURCE: MemCollab: Cross-Model Memory Collaboration via Contrastive Trajectory Distillation. Yurui Chang, Yiran Wu, Qingyun Wu, Lu Lin (Penn State, AG2AI). Marked "Preprint", arXiv:2603.23234v2 [cs.AI], 28 May 2026. No venue.
COVERAGE: All 80,486 chars read, including the appendices (A-F), tables, prompts and references. Figure 1 bar values and the Figure 3 curve are not in the text extraction, so I did not read them. I did not run the figure tool.

CLAIMS (ranked)
1. Naive cross-model memory transfer can hurt. A 32B agent's memory lowered the 7B agent below its no-memory baseline.
 number: 7B on MATH500 50.6 vs 52.2 vanilla; HumanEval 34.1 vs 42.7. For Llama-3-8B, 32B-memory gave MATH500 18.8 vs 27.4 and average 36.3 vs 41.7.
 setup: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, memory distilled from 32B trajectories in a BoT-style way. Memory built on 1000 train items, tested on 500 disjoint items per dataset (HumanEval is 164 tasks). Temperature 0, smolagents CodeAgent, seed 42.
 quote: "Using memory distilled solely from trajectories generated by the 32B-based agent (w/ Memory (32B)) degrades the performance of the 7B-based agent on MATH500 (50.6% vs. 52.2%) and HumanEval (34.1% vs. 42.7%)"
 where: Sec 3.1, Table 1 (about p.6)
2. Own-model memory helps modestly. Contrast-distilled shared memory beats it, and the gap is largest for the weaker agent.
 number: Qwen-7B average: vanilla 57.1, own memory 59.8, MemCollab 71.6. Qwen-32B average: 70.8, 75.6, 79.6. Llama-3-8B average: 41.7, 45.6, 53.9.
 setup: Table 1 and Table 2, four benchmarks (MATH500, GSM8K, MBPP, HumanEval), single run. Seed standard deviations are in Table 15.
 quote: "Qwen-2.5-7B ... w/ Memory (7B)60.0 86.2 50.2 42.7 59.8 ... MEMCOLLAB 67.0 87.4 57.6 74.4 71.6"
 where: Table 1, p.6
3. Contrasting trajectories from different models is what matters. Contrasting two samples from the same model recovers only part of the gain.
 number: Self-Contrast average for Qwen-7B is 67.5 vs MemCollab 71.6 (MATH500 58.4 vs 67.0). For Llama-3-8B, self-contrast is 45.0 vs 53.9.
 setup: Self-contrast uses two sampled outputs per task from one model. MemCollab pairs a preferred and an unpreferred trajectory from different models on the same task.
 quote: "self-contrast memory yields partial improvements, but remains inferior to MEMCOLLAB, underscoring the importance of cross-model contrast"
 where: Sec 3.1, Table 1
4. What is stored is distilled, not raw. Memory entries are abstract "enforce X; avoid Y" constraints, tagged with model-identity labels. No raw trajectories or solutions are kept.
 number: none for the form. Retrieval takes the top 3 entries (TF-IDF within the task-filtered subset), each contributing up to 3 constraints.
 quote: "The final memory bank M stores only normative, abstract reasoning constraints with preference-pair model labels, rather than raw trajectories, demonstrations, or final solutions."
 where: Sec 2.2; retrieval details in App B
 note: The preferred trajectory is the strongest model's, unless that model fails and another model succeeds. A correctness signal (verifier or ground truth) is needed at build time. Retrieval is task-category first, then model-aware: entries must involve the target model as either the winner or the loser.
5. Task-aware retrieval and the correctness signal both matter.
 number: Retrieval ablation, Fig 4: embedding 61.6 / 85.2 / 54.8 / 65.9 and prompting 63.4 / 84.2 / 55.2 / 62.1, against MemCollab 67.0 / 87.4 / 57.6 / 74.4 (MATH500 / GSM8K / MBPP / HumanEval). Preference selection on MBPP: default 57.6, random 50.2, reverse 52.9, vanilla 47.9.
 setup: Qwen2.5-7B. The Fig 4 bar values are partly ambiguous in the extraction, so check them against the figure before citing the pairing.
 quote: "MEMCOLLAB with the default rule achieves 57.6 on MBPP, compared with 50.2 for random selection and 52.9 for reverse selection."
 where: App D.1, Table 10
6. Gains hold across families and scales, and the agent finishes in fewer turns.
 number: Llama-3-70B with Qwen-7B (Table 4): MBPP 54.8 to 63.0 (self-memory 56.3), HumanEval 64.6 to 74.4. Comparable-scale Llama-3-70B with Qwen2.5-72B on MBPP (Table 7): 54.8 to 61.9 and 59.9 to 63.0. Average reasoning turns for Qwen-7B (Table 14): MBPP 3.1 to 1.4, HumanEval 3.3 to 1.5. AppWorld (Table 8) task goal completion: GPT-5-mini 47.7 to 63.3, GPT-5-nano 4.8 to 26.7. Adding a third model (Table 3) leaves the 7B at 67.0 to 66.8 and lifts the 32B from 73.8 to 75.0.
 quote: "MEMCOLLAB improves Llama-3-70B from 54.8 to 61.9 and Qwen2.5-72B from 59.9 to 63.0, outperforming both vanilla and self-memory baselines."
 where: App C, Tables 3, 7, 8, 14

BASELINES
- Vanilla: no memory.
- Single-agent memory: w/ Memory (own model) and w/ Memory (other model), both built BoT-style.
- Self-Contrast Memory.
- Buffer of Thoughts and Dynamic Cheatsheet, as published methods.
- Note that BoT's average beats own-model memory for Qwen-7B (63.0 vs 59.8). Dynamic Cheatsheet averages 56.8, below vanilla (57.1).

LIMITS
- The only stated limitation (App F) is that access control and safety filtering for shared memory are future work.
- Evidence is mostly Qwen2.5 and Llama-3 at 4B to 72B, on math and code benchmarks with a verifier. AppWorld uses GPT-5 mini and nano and was run without a Qwen comparison, because the 32B setup scored near zero there.
- It needs multiple models run on the training tasks, plus a correctness signal. An ASQA test replaced the signal with model self-selection: Qwen-7B 15.4 to 21.3, Qwen-32B 15.9 to 33.3 (Table 9).
- Seed standard deviations are reported only for the main configuration (Table 15), and the other tables are single runs. The 7B HumanEval vanilla standard deviation is 5.32, so small differences are noisy.
- Memory is evaluated on in-distribution tasks from the same benchmarks. Memory built from 1000 items and tested on 500 disjoint items from the same dataset, so transfer to new domains is not shown.
- The authors say the shared bank is "shared-bank, model-aware-retrieval", not model-agnostic: entries are tagged by model and retrieved only for the models involved. That is a caveat on the headline "shared memory" claim.
- Mechanism claims such as "suppressing model-specific bias" are an interpretation (the MemNCE view in App A is a proxy, not optimised). They are not tested by an experiment.
- The memory-quality judge is GPT-5-mini, with a 0.72 win rate for MemCollab vs 0.24 for Self-Memory.

BUILDS ON
- Buffer of Thoughts (Yang et al., NeurIPS 2024). Its extraction prompt is adapted, and it is also a baseline.
- Dynamic Cheatsheet (Suzgun et al., 2025, arXiv).
- ReasoningBank (Ouyang et al., 2025, arXiv).
- MemGPT (Packer et al., 2023), A-Mem (Xu et al., 2025), MemoryBank (Zhong et al., AAAI 2024), Mem1 and Memory-R1 (2025).
- Contrastive learning: InfoNCE / CPC (van den Oord et al., 2018) and Saunshi et al., ICML 2019, for the interpretation.
- Frameworks and benchmarks: smolagents CodeAgent, AppWorld (Trivedi et al., ACL 2024).
- The "prior paper" you mention (an agent's own memories helping more than another model's) is not named in the extraction. Figure 1 and Table 1 are the paper's own evidence for that pattern.

FIGURE CANDIDATE
- Figure 1 (p.2): "Accuracy on MATH500 dataset with memory from different resources." Bars for 7B and 32B: baseline, own-model memory, other-model memory, and MemCollab. It shows the transfer penalty and the fix in one picture. The bar values are not in the extraction, so read them from the image.

CODE: none. The pseudocode is Algorithm 1 (construction) and Algorithm 2 (retrieval). The memory entry format is "When ... , enforce ... ; avoid ...", from the contrast prompt in Table 18 (p.24).

PROBLEMS
- No embedded instructions found.
- Table 2 prose says Llama3-8B "reaches 74.4% on MATH500", but the table shows 42.4 for MATH500 and 74.4 for GSM8K. The prose is wrong, so do not cite it. Table 2 also lists the Qwen-32B MemCollab MATH500 as 70.6 while Table 1 gives 73.8, which suggests a different memory pairing.
- Figure 1 and Figure 3 values did not extract as numbers.
- Table cell spacing is garbled in places (columns run together). Numbers above were read by position, so recheck any you cite against the PDF.
